strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in EDA: fast RTL quality estimation to avoid costly logic synthesis iterations.
Constructs a large-scale dataset of 13,200 RTL designs with post-synthesis area and delay labels, enabling more reliable evaluation than prior small-scale studies.

Proposes a reasonable combination of graph self-supervised pretraining tasks (masked node modeling on post-GNN embeddings and edge prediction) tailored to CDFGs, and shows consistent improvements over no pretraining and over graph/LLM baselines.
Incorporates knowledge distillation from post-mapping netlists, which yields substantial gains across all methods and further boosts the proposed model.
Ablation studies demonstrate that both pretraining tasks contribute to performance, and the paper is generally well-organized and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The LLM baselines are used as frozen feature extractors without fine-tuning on the quality estimation task. A fine-tuned LLM could be a much stronger baseline, so the claim that structural learning inherently outperforms token-based learning is not convincingly established.

Masking post-GNN embeddings may leak information: the GNN processes the full graph (including the node to be masked) before masking, so the masked node's information can be propagated to neighbors and recovered by the Transformer. This makes the pretraining task easier and less effective for learning transferable representations; the paper does not analyze or ablate this design choice.

The directed Laplacian used for global positional embeddings (Eq. 2) is generally non-symmetric and may have complex eigenvalues/eigenvectors. The paper does not address how complex values are handled, which is a technical flaw.

Evaluation metrics are computed on log-transformed targets, but it is not specified whether the reported MAE, MAPE, R², and RRSE are on the log scale or the original scale. R² and MAPE on log scale can be misleading for practical quality estimation.
No statistical significance testing or error bars are provided; all results come from a single train/validation split, so the reported improvements may not be robust to random seed variation.

Scalability to large graphs is not discussed. The dataset contains designs with up to 19,169 nodes, yet the Transformer encoder has O(N²) attention. The paper does not explain how large graphs are handled (e.g., truncation, sampling, or subgraph processing), which is a critical omission for practical EDA use.

Reproducibility is limited: no hidden dimensions, parameter counts, or random seeds are reported; the code URL is missing in the manuscript; and the extraction of area/delay from post-mapping netlists (timing constraints, wire load models, clock period) is not specified.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing components (GNN + Transformer, masked node modeling, edge prediction, knowledge distillation) with minor adaptations for CDFGs. The paper does not compare to standard graph SSL baselines like GraphMAE or MaskGAE applied to CDFGs, so the necessity of the tailored pretraining tasks is not fully demonstrated.

The dataset is filtered (removing designs that fail CDFG conversion, synthesis, or simulation), which may bias results. The paper does not discuss the impact of filtering or the diversity of the retained designs.
The paper does not discuss limitations, failure cases, or generalization to unseen design styles, technology nodes, or hierarchical RTL designs.
The title 'Beyond Tokens' oversells the contribution: the method still uses token-like node features (type, width) as input.
The knowledge distillation strategy is inspired by prior work (VeriDistill), and its hyperparameters (e.g., τ, μ, layer choice for alignment) are not ablated.
The paper contains reference errors and typos (e.g., 'Grattafori' vs 'Grattafiori', year mismatches in the reference list), indicating insufficient proofreading.

strengths: Addresses a practically important EDA problem: fast pre-synthesis estimation of area and delay to shorten the slow RTL→netlist feedback loop, with clear industrial relevance.
Uses a substantially larger dataset (13,200 designs) than prior hand-crafted-feature work (<100 designs), which is a genuine step toward more credible training/evaluation.

The overall pipeline is reasonable and coherent: CDFG construction via Yosys/Stagira, GNN+Transformer encoder with Laplacian positional encodings, two self-supervised pretraining tasks, and cross-stage knowledge distillation from a post-mapping netlist predictor.

Includes ablations isolating the two pretraining objectives and compares against both graph-based (Graph-XGBoost, Graph-GNN) and LLM-based (CodeV variants) baselines, and the authors release code/data via an anonymous repository.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty for a general ML venue. Every component is off-the-shelf (GIN, Transformer encoder with Laplacian eigenvectors as in GraphGPS, GraphMAE/MaskGAE-style masking, class-balanced focal loss, and KD borrowed from VeriDistill). The only claimed novel element — masking post-GNN embeddings rather than raw features — is a minor tweak, and the stated rationale (masking raw nodes introduces 'ambiguity') is weakly argued and unsupported by any experiment isolating this choice.

The central 'beyond tokens' claim rests on comparisons to LLM baselines that are under-specified and potentially unfair. It is never stated whether the CodeV models are frozen feature extractors or fine-tuned, how token embeddings are pooled/aggregated, or how many parameters each predictor has. If the LLM side is a frozen-embedding + MLP pipeline while StructRTL is fully pretrained and fine-tuned, the headline gap is not a clean comparison of representations.

Table 2 is methodologically inconsistent. The only KD mechanism described aligns final-layer activations (z_CDFG^-1 vs z_PM^-1), which is impossible for Graph-XGBoost (a tree model) and undefined for the LLM baselines, yet the paper claims 'knowledge distillation improves the performance of all methods.' Either an undescribed distillation scheme was used for baselines, or the Table 2 comparison is not well-defined; this undermines a headline claim.

No held-out test set. The dataset is split only into train/validation (0.8/0.2), and results appear to be reported on the same set used for model selection and hyperparameter tuning (2,000 epochs, many tuned hyperparameters, 'trained until full convergence'). This inflates the reported R^2/MAE and prevents verification of generalization.

No variance, error bars, or significance testing across seeds. Several reported gains (e.g., the ablation deltas between StructRTL and its w/o-L_mnm / w/o-L_ep variants, ~0.01–0.02 R^2) are small enough that a single run cannot establish they are real.

Missing the most relevant baseline for the claimed contribution: applying standard GraphMAE/MaskGAE directly to CDFGs is never compared, so it is not established that the 'tailored' pretraining tasks are necessary rather than a re-labeling of existing masked graph modeling.

Dataset construction is vague and reproducibility is limited. 'Collect some existing Verilog datasets' gives no breakdown between VeriGen and DeepCircuitX, no deduplication discussion (GitHub-derived designs frequently contain near-duplicates/variants, risking train/val leakage), and filtering criteria such as 'meaningful outputs' are undefined. Model sizes, parameter counts, and training costs are also absent.

Overclaiming relative to evidence: only area and delay are evaluated despite claims about 'various quality estimation tasks,' and 'state-of-the-art' is asserted without statistical support. The abstract and introduction overstate the degree of novelty.

Presentation and reference-quality issues indicate limited care: multiple citation year mismatches (e.g., 'Hurst et al. (2022)' for a 2024 paper, 'Guo et al. (2020)' vs 2024, 'Li et al. (2025a)' for a 2023 paper, 'Liu et al. (2021)' for 2025c), and the KD section's description does not match how the baselines are treated.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical EDA problem: fast RTL-stage quality estimation for area and delay without invoking full synthesis for every design iteration.

The CDFG-based structural view is well motivated, and the two tailored self-supervised tasks—structure-aware masked node modeling and edge prediction—are sensible adaptations to computational graphs with strict semantics.
The method handles severe node-type class imbalance through stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss, which is a thoughtful design choice for CDFGs.

Experiments use a relatively large dataset of 13,200 designs and compare against both graph-based and LLM-based baselines, showing large empirical gains (e.g., ~0.1 R2 improvement over prior art in Table 1).
Ablations for the two pretraining tasks and results with/without knowledge distillation provide useful evidence for the main design choices.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with clear figures and algorithms that make the approach understandable.
Code and datasets are stated to be available in an anonymous repository, supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: There is no held-out test set: the dataset is split only into training and validation sets, and all results appear to be reported on the validation set. This risks optimistic estimates if validation was used for model selection or hyperparameter tuning, and it weakens the generalization claims.

The application of knowledge distillation to baselines in Table 2 is not described. It is unclear how non-neural baselines such as Graph-XGBoost or LLM-based baselines incorporate KD, making the claim that 'knowledge distillation enhances the performance of all methods' unsupported and the comparison potentially misleading.
No statistical significance tests or repeated runs with different seeds are reported. The repeated use of 'significantly outperforms' is therefore not statistically justified.

Baseline comparison could be stronger: the paper does not directly compare against the full VeriDistill method or MasterRTL, and the LLM baselines may not be tuned equivalently for the downstream regression task. The exclusion of MasterRTL due to SOG requiring synthesis is debatable, since the proposed CDFG construction also uses Yosys.

Dataset construction uses random splitting of designs collected from open-source repositories and textbooks, which may cause near-duplicate designs or similar modules to leak across train/validation splits, overestimating performance. Filtering by simulation and synthesizability may also introduce selection bias.

Ablations are limited: there is no study of architectural components (e.g., Transformer, positional embeddings, GNN depth), masking ratio, KD loss terms, or sensitivity to hyperparameters such as alpha, mu, and tau.

Scalability and computational cost are not discussed. Computing Laplacian eigenvectors for CDFGs with up to 19,169 nodes and training for 2,000 epochs could be expensive; the paper does not report runtime or complexity.
It is unclear whether evaluation metrics are computed on log-transformed or original area/delay values. This matters for comparability, especially for MAPE and MAE, and should be explicitly stated.
The paper lacks an explicit limitations section and does not discuss failure cases, generalization to industrial RTL styles, or the gap to the PM predictor beyond a brief acknowledgment.

strengths: Well-motivated shift from token-based to CDFG-based representations, with explicit reasoning about why structural semantics (operator connectivity, critical-path depth, reconvergence) are more directly aligned with area and delay than token sequences.

Novel and thoughtful design decision to apply masking at the level of post-GNN context-aware embeddings rather than raw node features/edges, correctly identifying that masking raw computational nodes (e.g., a plus operator) introduces ambiguity in CDFGs. This is a non-trivial adaptation of GraphMAE/MaskGAE to the circuit domain.

Comprehensive experimental suite: ablation of both pretraining tasks, architectural ablation (GNN-only, Transformer-only, no positional encoding, raw-feature masking), stratified-masking ablation, edge-ratio sensitivity, combinational/sequential split, functional and size-based generalization splits, LLM-on-CDFG comparison, fine-tuning comparison, and a pairwise industrial ranking study.

Demonstrated practical utility: 145x inference speedup over synthesis on 102 industrial modules and competitive ranking accuracy (82.35% area, 88.23% delay), which is a meaningful EDA contribution beyond benchmark numbers.

Honest and detailed limitations discussion (Appendix O) covering large-design scaling, sequential circuit weakness, and technology-node transfer, with a concrete register-boundary partitioning mitigation study.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: open-sourced code (as stated), explicit hyperparameters, dataset construction pipeline, and clear algorithmic pseudocode for stratified masking and class-balanced focal loss.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely compositional: the framework assembles well-known components (GIN + Transformer with Laplacian positional encodings, GraphMAE-style masked modeling, MaskGAE-style edge prediction) with domain-specific adaptations, and the knowledge distillation strategy is explicitly described as 'inspired by VeriDistill' (Moravej et al., 2025). The core methodological delta over prior work is incremental.

The central claim that the gains stem from 'structural semantics' being captured is not cleanly isolated. StructRTL differs from the LLM baselines in many ways simultaneously (architecture, training regime, parameter count, pretraining objective), so attributing the improvement specifically to the CDFG view is not fully supported by the experiments.

The knowledge distillation teacher requires logic synthesis and technology mapping (Yosys/ABC/SkyWater 130nm) to obtain the post-mapping netlist, so the 'no synthesis needed' framing is only true at inference; training still depends on the expensive synthesis pipeline, and it is not evaluated how sensitive results are to teacher quality or to different technology nodes.

Baseline fairness is questionable: the LLM baselines use frozen embeddings, which is justified by the fine-tuning overfitting result (Appendix K), but the comparison against 'Graph-GNN' and 'Graph-XGBoost' baselines appears relatively weak, and no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported despite claims of 'significantly outperforms' and 4-decimal metric reporting.

The industrial evaluation is small (51 design pairs / 102 modules) and the pairwise ranking setup differs from the regression metrics used elsewhere, making it difficult to calibrate how much of the 82-88% accuracy reflects genuine capability versus chance on a limited sample.

The paper reports that 5 L40 GPUs / ~42GB memory and ~40 hours on a single GPU are needed for convergence, and Appendix N shows 52GB peak memory for 20K-node designs, which is a nontrivial deployment constraint that somewhat undercuts the stated advantage over LLM-based pipelines; this trade-off could be discussed more candidly in the main text.
The code URL is missing/cut off in the manuscript ('open-sourced at'), which limits verifiability of the reproducibility claims.

Some claims in the abstract and introduction (e.g., CDFGs 'expose structural characteristics more explicitly, offering richer cues') are asserted rather than demonstrated, and the paper does not provide a controlled experiment that holds model capacity and pretraining fixed while only swapping token vs. graph views.

strengths: The problem is well-motivated and practically relevant: fast pre-synthesis area/delay estimation from RTL is a genuine need in the EDA flow, and the paper makes a coherent case that CDFGs expose structural semantics (operator connectivity, control/data dependencies, critical-path depth) that token-based LLM embeddings encode only implicitly.

The overall pipeline is sensible and internally consistent: CDFG construction via Yosys/RTLIL + AST traversal, GIN message passing, Laplacian-based global positional embeddings, a Transformer encoder, and joint mean/max graph pooling for regression are all reasonable choices, and the sign-flip handling of eigenvectors is a thoughtful detail.

The pretraining design shows some care for the domain: masking post-GNN context-aware embeddings rather than raw features, plus stratified masking (Algorithm 1) and class-balanced focal loss (Algorithm 2) to handle the severe 32-class node imbalance. The per-class analysis in Appendix D (e.g., Div/Mod/BitNXor accuracy collapsing without stratified masking) provides concrete evidence that these choices matter for rare but quality-critical operators.

The experimental suite is broad: two pretraining-task ablations, an architectural ablation (raw-feature masking, no positional encodings, GNN-only, Transformer-only), edge-sampling sensitivity, combinational vs. sequential splits, generalization across functionality (k-means over text embeddings) and across design size, LLM-on-CDFG, full LLM fine-tuning, runtime/memory scaling, and an industrial pairwise-ranking study.

The limitations discussion (Appendix O) is honest and specific (large-design degradation, weaker sequential performance, cross-technology-node generalization), and the register-boundary partitioning idea is a reasonable mitigation, even if preliminary.
Practical inference latency (0.096s vs. 13.97s synthesis, ~145x) is demonstrated, supporting the core 'fast feedback' motivation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The method is largely a recombination of existing components: GraphGPS-style GIN+Transformer with Laplacian positional encodings, GraphMAE-style masked reconstruction, MaskGAE-style edge prediction, and VeriDistill-style knowledge distillation. The genuinely new elements (masking post-GNN embeddings and stratified masking) are incremental, and the paper itself acknowledges the direct inspiration from these prior works.

No held-out test set and no statistical rigor. All results appear to be reported on the validation set, and every number is a single run with no variance, error bars, or significance tests. Yet the paper repeatedly claims StructRTL 'significantly outperforms' prior art; this central claim is not supported by any statistical evidence.

The baseline set is narrow and possibly under-representative. The comparison is essentially against frozen CodeV LLM embeddings (VeriDistill) and two graph baselines (Graph-XGBoost, Graph-GNN). MasterRTL is explicitly excluded via a 'scope' argument even though it is a directly relevant pre-synthesis PPA estimator, and no other recent graph-transformer or PPA-prediction methods are compared. The fairness of the LLM baselines (frozen backbone + mean pooling) relative to VeriDistill's actual method is also unclear.

Reporting ambiguity around the log transformation. Targets (area/delay) are log-transformed, and it is not made explicit whether MAE/MAPE/RRSE are computed in log space. This materially affects interpretation and cross-method comparability, and MAPE on log-transformed values is unusual. The claim that the transformation 'does not affect practical performance' is asserted rather than shown.

Absolute performance is moderate. The student model reaches R² ≈ 0.75–0.87 while the PM 'teacher' reaches 0.93–0.95, i.e., a large gap to the reference. This raises legitimate questions about whether the estimates are accurate enough for practical design-space exploration, and the KD gains, while consistent, do not close the gap.

The KD teacher is trivially strong by construction: the PM-based predictor operates on the post-mapping netlists from which the labels are derived, so its near-perfect accuracy is unsurprising. Consequently the KD results largely confirm that a strong same-stage model beats an RTL-stage model, which limits the informativeness of the KD experiment.

Reproducibility gaps. The manuscript states 'The code is open-sourced at' with no link. Dataset construction (four source datasets, filtering by CDFG conversion/synthesis/Verilator simulation) is described at a high level, but the exact filtering criteria, split seeds, and the log-space metric definitions are insufficiently specified to reproduce the reported numbers.

Scalability and cost concerns are under-addressed relative to the framing. Training requires ~40 hours on an L40 and ~42GB memory for 2000 epochs, and inference peak memory reaches 52.18GB at 20k nodes — exceeding the stated 46GB GPU — which is in tension with the 'near-instantaneous feedback' pitch. The register-boundary partitioning pilot actually reduces area ranking accuracy (82.35%→78.43%), so the scalability mitigation is not yet convincingly demonstrated.

The industrial evaluation is small (51 pairs / 102 modules) and is reported only as ranking accuracy for StructRTL, with no baseline comparison, so it cannot substantiate the claim of out-of-distribution superiority over prior art.

Several central results are deferred to appendices (architectural ablation, generalization, LLM-on-CDFG, partitioning), thinning the main-paper evidence for the headline 'new state-of-the-art' claim and making the main narrative rely heavily on supplementary material.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned contribution: the paper makes a convincing case that the CDFG view exposes structural semantics (control + data dependencies) that token-based LLM embeddings encode only implicitly, and it demonstrates this empirically with consistent gains on both area and delay prediction.

Extensive and multi-faceted evaluation: 13,200 designs, comparisons against graph-based (Graph-XGBoost, Graph-GNN) and three LLM-based VeriDistill variants, task ablations (w/o L_mnm, w/o L_ep), an architectural ablation (Appendix E), sensitivity analysis (Appendix F), combinational vs. sequential analysis (Appendix G), functional and size generalization splits (Appendices H, I), a limited-data study (Fig. 4), an industrial-design ranking evaluation, and LLM-on-CDFG and LLM fine-tuning studies (Appendices J, K).

The knowledge distillation from the PM-netlist teacher is a sensible cross-stage supervision mechanism, and the paper shows it improves not only StructRTL but also the baselines, giving a fair picture of its contribution rather than attributing all gains to KD.

Practical relevance and efficiency are demonstrated: a ~30M parameter model vs. ~7B LLM baselines, plus measured inference latency and memory scaling (Appendix N), making a credible case for near-instant feedback in design-space exploration.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (Appendix O) covering scalability, weaker performance on sequential circuits, and the unresolved cross-technology-node generalization problem, with a concrete register-boundary partitioning pilot study as a mitigation.
weaknesses: Potential information leakage in the structure-aware masked node modeling task. The GNN message-passing is performed on the full graph *before* masking, so the post-GNN embeddings of unmasked neighbors still contain messages aggregated from the masked node's true one-hot type. The Transformer can therefore partially recover the masked type from neighbor context, which may trivialize the pretraining signal and inflate the reported 82.27% accuracy. The paper motivates masking post-GNN embeddings by ambiguity of raw-feature masking but does not address this leakage path.

Limited methodological novelty. The core ingredients — masked node/attribute reconstruction, edge prediction, spectral positional encodings, and activation-matching KD — are adapted from existing graph SSL (GraphMAE, MaskGAE) and VeriDistill. The contribution is largely an application/adaptation to CDFGs, which is useful but incremental.

The reported 145x speedup (0.096s vs 13.97s synthesis) appears to measure only model inference and exclude the CDFG construction pipeline (Yosys compile to RTLIL + Stagira parser + AST traversal). Since Yosys is invoked during feature construction, the end-to-end speedup claim may be overstated; the paper also criticizes SOG for invoking synthesis while its own pipeline uses a synthesis tool.

The industrial evaluation (51 design pairs) is small and reported without confidence intervals or baseline comparison; the 82.35%/88.23% ranking accuracies are therefore hard to interpret statistically. Main tables (1, 2) likewise report single-split results without error bars or significance tests.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility concerns: LLM baselines are frozen with mean pooling and a 3-layer MLP, and the fine-tuning comparison (Table 11) shows severe overfitting, which may reflect suboptimal fine-tuning rather than an inherent limitation of token-based models. The code URL is missing ('The code is open-sourced at'), and reproducing the KD pipeline requires training and freezing the PM-based predictor in addition to the student.
